title: Implementing the public Backend protocol and publishing it as an entry point
surface: ascriptor.backends.base.Backend, Capabilities, ResourceLimits and Artifacts implemented by a class outside the library; discover() and get() over the ascriptor.backends entry-point group; compile_kernel(..., backend="<registered name>"); a pyproject.toml declaring that entry point
study_for: What a backend has to provide, as a list you can run: an instance of `Backend` returning `Capabilities`, `ResourceLimits` for a device, and `Artifacts` from a lowered module. Each is checked and reported on its own line, so 'it implements the protocol' is six verdicts rather than one claim.

The adapter is transparent on purpose. It delegates every instruction to CCE and its emitted files and entry symbol are compared byte for byte against CCE's own -- so what the example demonstrates is the *protocol*, with the lowering held fixed. A backend that actually lowered differently would need its own semantic and vendor compilation gates, and nothing here would stand in for them.

The one thing the adapter adds is a `teaching_adapter` key in the artifact metadata, and that is checked too. It is the seam where a real backend would record what it did, and it is the only difference the artifact comparison is allowed to have.

Discovery is exercised the standard way -- `discover()` and `get()` over the `ascriptor.backends` entry-point group -- using temporary distribution metadata placed on this process's import path. Nothing is installed, no dependency is touched, and the directory is removed when the check ends. `pyproject.toml` is the file that shows what an installed distribution would publish, and `main.py` checks that it declares the same group, name and object path that the temporary metadata used. Otherwise the two could drift and the example would be demonstrating discovery of something nobody could install.

A conformance claim gets one numerical result behind it: the copy kernel runs through the *registered name* and its output is compared to the input bitwise. The kernel is a copy so that the backend is the only variable -- a difference is the backend's.
`check_domain` requires the reference not to alias the input. For a copy that matters: a kernel that handed back the caller's own tensor would compare equal for the wrong reason.
do_not_copy_when: You are adding an instruction rather than adapting one. This example establishes protocol conformance and discovery only; a new lowering needs its own numerical references, its own vendor compilation and its own hardware evidence.
You expect the capabilities or limits to be yours. They are CCE's, returned unchanged. A backend for different hardware has to answer those questions itself, and this example says nothing about how.

You are treating the temporary metadata as an installation. It exists for the duration of one check and is on this process's path only. Ship the `pyproject.toml` entry point if you want a backend others can discover.

You are reading a model run as backend execution. `sim` and `pipesim` run the library's own models; the backend's own compilation and execution are separate stages, and only the non-model launchers reach them.
